Gunfire, by County

Four years of reported shootings placed in the county where they happened and counted per person, laid beside the CDC's count of firearm deaths, every mass shooting through November 2026, and a decade of fatal police shootings. The map of where people are shot is a map of cities. The map of where they die of it is not.

Shall and may: four questions for every number

Every number in this series ends a chain of people who held something: the gun, the warning, the wound, the record. Law gives some of them duties and others powers. A duty, written with shall, binds every county alike and makes a floor. A power, written with may, is used where someone chooses to use it, and makes a map.

  1. Who holds it?Name the office or the owner.
  2. Shall or may?A duty everyone carries, or a choice someone makes.
  3. Who keeps the count?And what does nobody count.
  4. Who is left with the remainderwhen the holder does nothing.

On this page the third question comes first, which is why the map views above are grouped by who kept the count. A nonprofit archive reads the news and police logs, and nobody is obliged to tell it anything. Coroners and medical examiners must rule on every violent death, and the CDC adds up their certificates. A newspaper counted the people police shot dead for ten years and then stopped.

What the county map shows

Every incident in the Gun Violence Archive with a location was placed in its county by its coordinates. People shot means killed or wounded. Rates divide by the county's 2014 to 2018 population and by four years. Counties are grouped by how many people live on a square mile, from the 150 big-city counties above a thousand to the 576 frontier counties below ten. Two newer counts sit beside the archive: the CDC's tally of every firearm death, 2018 to 2022, and the archive's running list of mass shootings, kept up to 3 November 2026. Each finding names whose count it rests on.

Per person, the map moves south.

The 25 counties with the most shootings hold 16% of the population and 35% of the people shot; Cook County alone had 12,950. Counted per person, a different country comes forward. The city of St. Louis had 179 people shot per 100,000 residents a year, New Orleans 150, Baltimore 129; the national figure is 12.5. Behind them are not the biggest cities but the second cities of the South and the independent cities of Virginia: Richmond; Jackson and Meridian in Mississippi; Shreveport; Macon, Columbus and Savannah in Georgia; Portsmouth, Norfolk, Newport News and Hampton. Lauderdale County, Mississippi, population 77,000, had a higher rate than Cook County.

Gunfire thins out with the people. Dying of it does not.

In the 150 counties with more than a thousand people per square mile, 17 people per 100,000 were shot each year. In the 576 frontier counties with fewer than ten, 5.5 were. The death rate fell much less, from 5.2 to 3.2 per 100,000, because the share of the wounded who died rose at every step: 29% in big-city counties, 33% in suburban ones, 38% in small-town counties, 46% in rural ones, 56% on the frontier. The kind of shooting changes with the landscape. In big-city counties one death in ten came from domestic violence and one in fourteen from a police shooting; on the frontier it was three in ten and nearly one in four. But even street shootings, with the domestic, the accidental and the police cases set aside, killed 27% of their victims in the cities and 51% in the emptiest counties, where the nearest trauma center can be hours away.

The CDC's map is not the archive's map.

The archive counts shootings that made the news or a police log. The CDC counts death certificates. For 2018 to 2022 it reports 216,703 firearm deaths in the 2,297 counties that had at least ten, 13.6 per 100,000 a year, and that count runs the opposite way across the landscape. Big-city counties had 12.0 firearm deaths per 100,000 a year; suburban 13.0; small-town 15.0; rural 19.4; frontier 24.5. The archive's killed rate for 2014 to 2017 fell from 5.2 to 3.2 along the same line. What fills the gap is suicide. Suicides by every method rose from 11.1 per 100,000 in big-city counties to 30.6 on the frontier, while homicides stayed between 5.7 and 9.3 in every class. Among the counties with at least 50,000 people the two maps still rank alike at the top, with a rank correlation of 0.67: St. Louis city, Hinds County around Jackson, New Orleans and Baltimore lead the CDC's list as they led the archive's. Lower down they part. Gila County, Arizona, east of Phoenix, had 40 firearm deaths per 100,000 a year by the CDC's count, more than Philadelphia or Chicago; in the archive's four years it had 1.9. Elko County, Nevada, had 34 and 3.8. In those counties the gun deaths are suicides, and the archive, which hears gunfire through the news, hears almost none of them.

The border that matters is the one a county map hides.

Counties count the dead. States write the gun law. A 2025 study in JAMA Pediatrics sorted the states into three groups by the strictness of their firearm laws since 2010: eight strict, eleven permissive, thirty most permissive. Laid over the CDC's county counts for 2018 to 2022, that grouping shows through every kind of county. Big-city counties in the strict states had 7.3 firearm deaths per 100,000 residents a year, and big-city counties in the most permissive states 16.9. Suburban counties had 7.8 and 15.1, small-town counties 10.2 and 16.9, rural counties 12.2 and 20.8. The average rural county in a strict state had a lower rate than the average big-city county in a permissive one.

The same thing shows at the line itself. Forty stretches of state border separate states in different groups. Take only the counties that touch the line. On 29 of the 40, the looser side has the higher rate, and on 15 of the 17 borders of a strict state. Pooled, the border counties on the strict side had 10.4 firearm deaths per 100,000 a year and their neighbours across the line 16.0. New Hampshire's border counties had 9.5 against 2.5 in the Massachusetts counties they touch, Arizona's 23.5 against California's 10.1, Missouri's 24.9 against Illinois's 15.5.

This describes; it does not rule on any law. The strict states are also richer and more urban and own fewer guns, and ownership is one of the things the laws act on. The border counties are not twins: Philadelphia sits on the Pennsylvania side of New Jersey's line. And the grouping has exceptions both ways. Maryland's border counties had higher rates than the Virginia and Pennsylvania counties across from them. Illinois and Maryland, both strict, had about 13 deaths per 100,000 statewide, nearer the permissive group's 13.9 than their own group's 7.9. People who doubt that law explains the gap point to those confounders and exceptions. The studies that try to isolate one law at a time, summarised in the Lake County chapter, find support for some laws and little evidence either way for others.

Poverty is the gradient inside every kind of county.

Sort the counties of each density class by their poverty rate and the least poor fifth look alike everywhere: about 4 people shot per 100,000 a year, whether the county is a big city or open range. The poorest fifth do not. In big-city counties the poorest fifth had 31 people shot per 100,000, eight times the least poor; in suburban counties 21, in small-town counties 14, in rural counties 12, on the frontier 7.5. Poverty's gradient is steepest where people are closest together.

Police shootings keep a different map.

Fatal shootings by police run the other way across the landscape: 0.25 per 100,000 a year in big-city counties, 0.52 on the frontier. Among the 594 counties with at least 100,000 people, the highest rates are in the Mountain West and on the Plains: Pueblo, Colorado; Pennington County, South Dakota, around Rapid City; Potter County, Texas, around Amarillo; Coconino County, Arizona; Yellowstone County, Montana; Bernalillo County, New Mexico. Across those 594 counties the two rates are only loosely related, with a rank correlation of 0.37. The places where the police shoot the most people are not, for the most part, the places where the most people are shot.

Mass shootings, counted to this week.

The archive keeps a separate list of incidents in which four or more people were shot, not counting the shooter, and keeps it current. From 1 January 2013 to 3 November 2026 it holds 6,281 of them, with 6,267 people killed and 26,212 wounded; all but nine could be placed in a county. They rose from about 300 a year to 689 in 2021, fell for three years to 503 in 2024 and 415 in 2025, and have turned up again: 423 by 3 November this year, against 373 by the same date last year, 449 the year before and 590 in 2023. They are the most urban form of gunfire in this atlas. Big-city counties, with 40% of the country's people, had 59% of its mass shootings, 2.1 per million residents a year against 0.3 on the frontier, and 2,258 of the 3,142 counties have had none in fourteen years. Ten counties account for a quarter of them, led by Cook County with 465, Philadelphia with 189 and Los Angeles with 173. Per person the list is the archive's list again: St. Louis city with 21 a year per million people, New Orleans 19, Baltimore 14, Caddo Parish around Shreveport 12, the District of Columbia 11, Hinds County 10.

Where gunfire is counted but no one is hit.

The archive also records incidents in which shots were fired and nobody was struck, 35,550 of them in these four years. They are a map of police practice, not of gunfire. Peoria County, Illinois, logged 57 such incidents per 100,000 a year, more than any big city, followed by Black Hawk County, Iowa, Boone County, Missouri, and Duval County, Florida. Where a department publishes its shots-fired calls, or runs acoustic sensors, the archive hears them; elsewhere the same gunfire goes unheard. The map above can be switched to this measure. Read it as a map of listening.

What kills, against what gets a map.

In 2024, the last year with final death certificates, 44,447 Americans died by gunfire: 27,593 by suicide, 15,364 by homicide, 636 shot by law enforcement, 450 by accident and 404 with the intent undetermined. Mass shootings, as the archive defines them, killed 511 people that year, a little over one death in a hundred. Until this edition the atlas gave mass shootings one of its seven map views and suicide none. Suicide and homicide by every method now have views of their own.

Who keeps the count, and what nobody counts.

Each of the three record-keepers decides what the country can know about its gunfire.

The archive. The Gun Violence Archive is a nonprofit that compiles incidents from news and police reports. Nobody is required to report to it, so it records what gets reported. Over 2014 to 2017 it logged 56,618 deaths, close to the CDC's count of about 53,000 firearm homicides for those years and far below the CDC's roughly 148,000 firearm deaths of all kinds, because suicides, three fifths of American gun deaths, rarely make the news. The 2,297 suicides it does record are left out of the lethality figures here. The archive does not publish its incident records in bulk. The last complete public copy was assembled by a volunteer in March 2018, which is why the incident layers stop at 2017 while the mass-shooting list, which the archive does publish, runs to this month.

The certificate. Death certificates are the one count the law requires. A coroner or medical examiner must rule on every violent death, and the CDC adds up the rulings. The count is complete and slow: final figures for 2024 arrived in 2026. The CDC withholds any county with fewer than ten deaths, which leaves 845 counties, with 3% of the population, off the firearm map, and it reports Connecticut by planning region, which leaves that state grey.

The newspaper. The Washington Post counted every fatal police shooting from 2015 and closed the count at the end of 2024. Its count for that last year was 1,175. Death certificates for the same year recorded 636 people shot dead by law enforcement, and the Post's own notes say the FBI's collection captured about a third of departments' fatal shootings in 2021.

Nobody keeps these for every county:

  • the people wounded by gunfire and not killed. The archive's news count is the only national one;
  • shots fired that hit no one, outside the places that publish them;
  • people shot dead by police after 2024, in any series this atlas can use;
  • where the guns used in crimes were first sold. The ATF traces them and publishes summaries by state.

Small counties have few incidents and unstable rates, so the map leaves a county grey until it has at least five people shot, twenty for the share who died, three fatal police shootings, three mass shootings, or five shots-fired incidents. Of 225,597 incidents, 97% carried coordinates and were placed by them; the rest are not on the map.

This edition, 9 November 2026.

The atlas was reviewed against the four questions at the top of the page. Three things changed. The map views are grouped by record-keeper, and suicide and homicide by every method have their own views, because the old set of views followed the news and the news follows the rare death. A new finding sets each county against the law of its state, because a county map hides the border where the law changes. And the notes on data now say who decided what is counted, and list what nobody counts.

Still missing: incident records after 2017, any county measure of gun ownership, and the wounded. The first of the four questions, who holds what, is hard to answer for 3,142 counties at once. The Lake County chapter answers it for one, and the chapter on that county's hospitals follows the wound.

Every county

Rates are per 100,000 residents a year. Share who died is among people shot in 2014 to 2017, excluding suicides, and is blank below 20 people shot. CDC firearm deaths and suicides (2018 to 2022) and homicides (2016 to 2022) are blank where a county had fewer than ten. Police shootings cover 2015 to 2024; mass shootings cover 2013 to 3 November 2026.

Method and sources

Incidents

The Gun Violence Archive's incident records from 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2017, as mirrored on GitHub in 2018: 225,597 incidents with the number killed and injured, coordinates, and the archive's incident tags. People shot is killed plus injured. An incident tagged as a suicide with one person killed and nobody injured is a lone suicide and is removed from the lethality figures. Street shootings are incidents with none of the tags for police involvement, domestic violence, murder-suicide, accidental discharge or suicide. Shots fired, no one hit, is the archive's own tag.

Counties and people

Incidents were assigned to counties by point-in-polygon against the Census cartographic county boundaries; 97% had usable coordinates. Population, land area and poverty rates are 2014 to 2018 American Community Survey estimates as packaged in the CDC and ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index 2018, summed or population-weighted from census tracts. Density is people per square mile of land. Fatal police shootings are the Washington Post's database, 2015 to 2024, placed by coordinates where given (89%) and by county name otherwise; 92% could be placed.

Comparisons

Density classes split counties at 1,000, 250, 50 and 10 people per square mile. Poverty fifths are drawn within each class so that each fifth holds a fifth of the class's population. Intervals on shares are Wilson 95% intervals; intervals on rates are exact Poisson 95% intervals on the count. The rank correlations are Spearman's: police against people shot over the 594 counties with at least 100,000 residents, and CDC firearm deaths against the archive's killed rate over the 975 counties with at least 50,000 residents and a reported CDC rate.

The state line

State law groups are those of Faust and colleagues, JAMA Pediatrics, 2025, as listed in the paper's preprint: strict (California, Connecticut, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island), permissive (Colorado, Delaware, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Vermont, Virginia, Washington) and most permissive (the other thirty; Hawaii is not grouped). Rates sum deaths and person-years over the counties that report. Border counties are those sharing a boundary segment with a county of the neighbouring state in the Census cartographic boundaries; each of the 40 borders between states in different groups is compared once, and a county on two such borders is counted on both. Suicides are the CDC's all-method counts for 2018 to 2022 and homicides its all-method counts for 2016 to 2022, both withheld below ten deaths; national figures shown with those maps cover the reporting counties, which hold 99% and 89% of the population.

Deaths and mass shootings

Firearm deaths, suicides and homicides are the National Center for Health Statistics' county counts for 2018 to 2022, as released in the 2025 County Health Rankings: deaths of all intents involving a firearm, and suicides and homicides by every method, each divided by five years of population. The CDC withholds counties with fewer than ten deaths, so 845 counties, holding 3% of the population, have no firearm rate; class rates are computed over the counties that report, and the frontier figure in particular rests on 57% of frontier residents. Connecticut's counts are released for its planning regions and could not be assigned to its counties. Mass shootings are the archive's own list, four or more people shot excluding the shooter, from 1 January 2013 to 3 November 2026, taken from a daily mirror that geocodes each address; 99.9% could be placed in a county. Mass-shooting rates divide by 2023 population and by 13.84 years. The map leaves a county grey below three mass shootings.
